{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

Quarto documents are rendered on your own computer, so the downloadable project at the bottom of this page is the main practice for Chapter 16: a small Quarto project with Elaf's results chapter, a parameterised faculty report, and the Shiny dashboard. The exercises below practise the R side of reproducible reporting in your browser: writing results into sentences, making tables, and checking data before sharing it. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
students  <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
```

## Numbers in sentences

### Exercise 1: A sentence that writes itself

Inline code in a Quarto document puts the result of R code into a sentence. `paste0()` does the same in the Console. Complete the sentence so that it reports the number of students and the number of faculties.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
paste0("The sample included ", nrow(students), " graduate students from ",
       n_distinct(students$______), " faculties.")
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
paste0("The sample included ", nrow(students), " graduate students from ",
       n_distinct(students$faculty), " faculties.")
```

"The sample included 600 graduate students from 5 faculties." In a Quarto document, the same numbers would be written with inline code, so they update whenever the data changes.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Rounding for the reader

Calculate the mean wellbeing in the first semester and report it rounded to one decimal place. `sprintf("%.1f", x)` always shows exactly one decimal place, even when it is zero, which `round()` does not.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
first <- semesters |> filter(semester == 1)
m <- mean(first$wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE)
m
round(m, 1)
sprintf("Average wellbeing was %s (SD %s).",
        sprintf("%.1f", m), sprintf("%.1f", sd(first$______, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sprintf("Average wellbeing was %s (SD %s).",
        sprintf("%.1f", m), sprintf("%.1f", sd(first$wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

"Average wellbeing was 60.5 (SD 12.0)." `round(12.0, 1)` would print `12`, dropping the decimal; `sprintf("%.1f", ...)` keeps it, as journals expect.
:::
:::

## Tables

### Exercise 3: A results table

Summarise first-semester wellbeing by faculty, then turn the result into a formatted table with `knitr::kable()`, with one decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
semesters |>
  filter(semester == 1) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |>
  summarise(Students = n(),
            Mean = mean(wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE),
            SD = sd(wellbeing, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = faculty) |>
  arrange(faculty) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = ______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

In the browser, `kable()` prints a plain-text table; in a rendered Quarto document, the same code produces a formatted, numbered table.
:::
:::

## Before sharing data

### Exercise 4: Small cells

Count the students in each combination of faculty, study mode, gender, and having children, and show the combinations with fewer than 5 students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
students |>
  count(faculty, study_mode, gender, has_children) |>
  filter(n < ______) |>
  arrange(n)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
  filter(n < 5) |>
```

Five combinations describe only three or four students each, all of them part-time students with children. Anyone who knows the department might recognise them.
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: Protecting the small cells

Leave `has_children` out of the combination and count again. What is the smallest group now?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
students |>
  count(faculty, study_mode, ______) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  head(3)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
students |>
  count(faculty, study_mode, gender) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  head(3)
```

Without `has_children`, the smallest groups are much larger. Removing (or grouping) one variable that the analysis does not need is often enough to protect participants before sharing.
:::
:::

## Recording versions

### Exercise 6: What am I running?

Report the version of R and of the dplyr package. (In the browser, R runs through webR, so the versions may differ from your computer's.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
R.version.string
packageVersion("______")
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
R.version.string
packageVersion("dplyr")
```

These are the numbers to report in a methods section, together with a citation for each key package from `citation("dplyr")`.
:::
:::

## Work on your own computer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Download the Chapter 16 project

A small Quarto project: `results.qmd`, Elaf's results chapter with inline numbers, a numbered table and figure, and citations; `faculty-report.qmd`, a report with a faculty parameter; and `app.R`, the wellbeing dashboard. The exercises ask you to extend each of them, and the `solutions` folder has finished versions. You need Quarto (it comes with RStudio) and the packages listed in `README.txt`.

- [Download chapter16.zip](chapter16.zip), unzip it, and double-click `chapter16.Rproj`.
- Or type this one line in RStudio's Console:

```r
usethis::use_course("https://polla-fattah.github.io/R4NTR/playground/chapter16.zip")
```
:::
